sections.overview: Aequorea victoria is a nearly transparent hydromedusa of the northeastern Pacific. Its delicate bell and marginal tentacles make it difficult to see in water, but its light-producing system made the species famous in biomedical science: the green fluorescent protein GFP was first isolated from it. The jelly also produces blue-green bioluminescence when mechanically disturbed. GFP fluorescence and the animal’s emitted light are related but distinct phenomena.
sections.identification: The medusa has a clear, rounded bell with many fine tentacles along its margin and a central mouth bordered by broad oral lobes. Its nearly glasslike transparency is the main field character; the internal radial canals and gonads may be visible through the bell. It is often only a few centimetres across, but museum and aquarium accounts report adults reaching about 25 cm in bell diameter. These values vary with age, food and locality. No reliable body mass, bell height, or male–female size comparison was found. It can be confused with other transparent hydromedusae, so use tentacle arrangement, marginal structures, radial canals and geographic range rather than transparency alone.
sections.habitat: It lives in coastal and offshore waters of the northeastern Pacific, from southern California north toward British Columbia and Vancouver Island. The medusa drifts and swims in the plankton, while the much less studied hydroid stage attaches to the seafloor or hard surfaces such as shells. Seasonal abundance varies, and medusae may be particularly visible in spring and summer in parts of the Salish Sea.
sections.diet: It captures planktonic animals with its tentacles and oral lobes. Copepods and other small crustaceans are eaten, but field and laboratory observations show a strong preference for gelatinous prey, including comb jellies and smaller hydromedusae. Its mouth can expand to engulf prey that is large relative to the bell. Its own bioluminescent substrate, coelenterazine, must be obtained through food rather than synthesized from scratch, according to experimental work.
sections.behavior: The medusa pulses its bell to swim and also drifts with currents. Mechanical disturbance triggers brief blue-green flashes from photoproteins concentrated around the bell margin; light production may startle or confuse predators, though its defensive effectiveness varies by context. Aequorea is an active predator of gelatinous plankton rather than simply a passive drifting filter feeder.
sections.reproduction: The sexes are separate. Adult medusae release eggs or sperm into the water, where fertilization produces a swimming planula larva. The planula settles and grows into a benthic hydroid colony, which later buds off young medusae asexually. In the Puget Sound region, small medusae bud from colonies in early spring; seasonal timing elsewhere is less well documented. The hydroid stage remains poorly known in the wild.
sections.ecology: As a predator of gelatinous plankton and small crustaceans, it links planktonic food webs and can itself become prey for larger animals such as ocean sunfish. Its population abundance may vary sharply among years and locations. The species is also a source of aequorin and GFP, but laboratory use of these molecules does not represent the jelly’s ecological role.
sections.conservation: The sources reviewed do not provide a global IUCN assessment or population trend specific to Aequorea victoria. It is a widespread northeastern Pacific species, but local population fluctuations and limited monitoring make a simple abundance claim unreliable. It is not known as a species of conservation concern in the references reviewed.
